paper-title: The Head Domain of Plakophilin-1 Binds to Desmoplakin and Enhances Its Recruitment to Desmosomes_ IMPLICATIONS FOR CUTANEOUS DISEASE - ScienceDirect 

      JavaScript is disabled on your browser.
      Please enable JavaScript to use all the features on this page.
      Skip to main contentSkip to articleScienceDirectJournals & BooksHelpSearchMy accountTata Institute of Fundamental ResearchView PDFDownload full issueSearch ScienceDirectOutlineEXPERIMENTAL PROCEDURESRESULTSDISCUSSIONAcknowledgmentsREFERENCESCited by (127)Figures (5)Journal of Biological ChemistryVolume 274, Issue 26, 25 June 1999, Pages 18145-18148COMMUNICATIONThe Head Domain of Plakophilin-1 Binds to Desmoplakin and Enhances Its Recruitment to Desmosomes: IMPLICATIONS FOR CUTANEOUS DISEASE*Author links open overlay panelAndrew P.Kowalczyk‡§, MechthildHatzfeld¶, Elayne A.Bornslaeger‖, Daniel S.Kopp‖, Jeffrey E.Borgwardt‖, Connie M.Corcoran‖, AaronSettler‖, Kathleen J.Green‡‖Show moreOutlineAdd to MendeleyShareCitehttps://doi.org/10.1074/jbc.274.26.18145Get rights and contentUnder a Creative Commons licenseopen accessThe contribution of desmosomes to epidermal integrity is evident in the inherited blistering disorder associated with the absence of a functional gene for plakophilin-1. To define the function of plakophilin-1 in desmosome assembly, interactions among the desmosomal cadherins, desmoplakin, and the armadillo family members plakoglobin and plakophilin-1 were examined. In transient expression assays, plakophilin-1 formed complexes with a desmoplakin amino-terminal domain and enhanced its recruitment to cell-cell borders; this recruitment was not dependent on the equimolar expression of desmosomal cadherins. In contrast to desmoplakin-plakoglobin interactions, the interaction between desmoplakin and plakophilin-1 was not mediated by the armadillo repeat domain of plakophilin-1 but by the non-armadillo head domain, as assessed by yeast two-hybrid and recruitment assays. We propose a model whereby plakoglobin serves as a linker between the cadherins and desmoplakin, whereas plakophilin-1 enhances lateral interactions between desmoplakin molecules. This model suggests that epidermal lesions in patients lacking plakophilin-1 are a consequence of the loss of integrity resulting from a decrease in binding sites for desmoplakin and intermediate filaments at desmosomes.Previous article in issueNext article in issueDesmosomes are intercellular adhesive junctions that act as anchorage points for intermediate filament networks. The desmosomal cadherins, desmogleins and desmocollins, bind directly to the cytoplasmic protein plakoglobin (1, 2, 3), a member of the armadillo gene family that includes the adherens junction protein β-catenin (4). The desmosomal cadherin-plakoglobin complex is coupled to the intermediate filament network by desmoplakin (5, 6), which binds to both plakoglobin and intermediate filaments (7, 8, 9, 10).The disruption of desmosomes by gene ablation in experimental model systems (6, 11, 12, 13) or by autoimmune antibodies in human patients (14) severely compromises tissue integrity and function. Recently, the first human genetic disorders involving mutations in desmosomal genes have been reported. Haploinsufficiency of desmoplakin results in the disruption of intermediate filament interactions with desmosomes in palmoplantar epidermis (15). In addition, mutation of both alleles of plakophilin-1 (PKP-1)1and consequent loss of the protein causes epidermal fragility, perturbed desmoplakin localization, and detachment of intermediate filaments from the plasma membrane of keratinocytes (16). PKP-1 was originally identified as Band 6, a 75-kDa keratin-associated protein component of desmosomes in stratified tissues (17). PKP-1 is also part of the armadillo gene family (18, 19, 20, 21, 22). In overlay assays, PKP-1 was recently found to bind to a number of desmosomal components, including desmoplakin and intermediate filament polypeptides (10). However, the mechanism by which PKP-1 contributes to desmosome assembly and attachment to intermediate filaments remains unknown.We report here that the non-armadillo head domain of PKP-1 binds directly to the amino-terminal domain of desmoplakin and enhances its recruitment to cell junctions. Our data indicate that PKP-1 is a desmoplakin-binding partner in the desmosomal plaque and suggest a model by which PKP-1 recruits desmoplakin to desmosomes by increasing lateral interactions between junction components.EXPERIMENTAL PROCEDURESCell Culture and ImmunofluorescenceCOS 7 cells (subclone 20) were transiently transfected and processed for immunofluorescence analysis as described (8, 23). To enhance detection of full-length PKP-1 and the PKP-1 head domain, cells were permeabilized with 0.01% saponin before fixation in methanol (24). DP-NTP was detected using the monoclonal antibody M2 directed against the FLAG epitope tag (Eastman Kodak Co., Rochester, NY). Rabbit polyclonal antibodies against recombinant PKP-1 head (Ab 667) and repeat domains (Ab 670)2 were used to detect the PKP-1 fragments.cDNA Expression ConstructsA cDNA encoding the first 584 amino acids of desmoplakin (DP-NTP), and an amino-terminally FLAG epitope-tagged version driven by the CMV promoter were described previously (5, 8, 25). DP-NTP with a carboxyl-terminal FLAG tag was generated by PCR, cloned into pBluescript and sequenced, and then subcloned into the CMV expression vector. Full-length, Myc-tagged plakoglobin and Dsg1 were described previously (8), and the full-length “a” form of PKP-1 was assembled and cloned into pCMV-Script (Stratagene, La Jolla, CA) (19). Plasmids encoding the PKP-1 head and armadillo repeat domains were generated by reverse transcription-PCR using RNA isolated from A431 cells. The resulting cDNAs were sequenced and subcloned into the pCMV5 vector (26) using theBamHI and HindIII restriction sites. The PKP-1 head domain comprises amino acids 1–286 (ending with QVYQL) and the repeat domain begins at amino acid 287 (GGICK).Co-immunoprecipitation and Immunoblot AnalysisCo-immunoprecipitation was carried out as described previously (8, 23). Monoclonal antibody M2 coupled to agarose beads (Kodak) was used to capture FLAG epitope-tagged DP-NTP. Antibodies to plakoglobin (mouse mAb 11E4) (27) and PKP-1 (rabbit polyclonal Ab 667) were used to precipitate these armadillo proteins and associated polypeptides. Immune complexes were released by incubation in reducing SDS-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis sample buffer at 95 °C and analyzed by immunoblot using Enhanced Chemiluminescence (Amersham Pharmacia Biotech). Plakoglobin was detected using mAb 11E4, DP-NTP was detected using a rabbit polyclonal antibody NW161 (5), and desmoglein (Dsg1) was monitored using mAb 9E10 directed against the Myc tag (28).Yeast Two-hybrid Constructs and AssaysDP-NTP in pACTII was generated as described previously (8). The desmocollin 2a (Dsc2a) cytoplasmic tail in pACTII was generated by PCR to include nucleotides 2198–2743 (nucleotide numbering according to Ref. 29). The PKP-1 constructs described above were subcloned into the DNA-binding domain vector pBD-Gal4 (Stratagene) using EcoRI and SalI restriction sites. The Dsg1 cytoplasmic domain encoding amino acids 568–1049 (MICC … QYSK) was amplified by PCR and cloned into the pGAD 424 vector (CLONTECH). The clone contains a single amino acid exchange (amino acids Glu625 → Gly) compared with the published sequence (GenBankTM accession number X56654). To assay for interactions between proteins, yeast (strain HF7c) were transformed with constructs of interest, and β-galactosidase activity was monitored using 4-methylumbelliferyl β-d-galactopyranoside as a substrate (9, 23). Transformants were also tested for growth in the absence of histidine using 25 mm 3-aminotriazole, and growth was monitored spectrophotometrically (A600) as an assay for protein interactions.RESULTSPKP-1 Enhances Desmoplakin Recruitment to Intercellular JunctionsTo determine the molecular basis of the cutaneous lesions exhibited by patients lacking PKP-1, the role of PKP-1 in desmosome assembly was addressed by transiently expressing junctional proteins in COS cells. We previously demonstrated that a polypeptide comprising the first 584 amino acids of desmoplakin (DP-NTP) is recruited to cell borders when co-expressed with a cadherin and plakoglobin (8, 23). Here, DP-NTP was expressed alone (Fig.1, A and B) or in combination with full-length PKP-1 (Fig. 1, C andD). When expressed alone, DP-NTP remained in large cytoplasmic aggregates and exhibited minimal cell border localization (Fig. 1A). In the presence of PKP-1, extensive DP-NTP recruitment to intercellular junctions was observed (Fig.1C), and PKP-1 and DP-NTP co-localized at cell borders (Fig.1D). Nuclear staining was also observed for PKP-1, consistent with a report that PKP-1 is present in the nucleus in many cell types (24).Download: Download full-size imageFigure 1. PKP-1 enhances recruitment of the desmoplakin amino-terminal domain to cell borders.COS cells were transiently transfected (T) with DP-NTP alone (A andB) or in the presence of PKP-1 (C andD) or the PKP-1 head (E and F) or armadillo repeat domain (Arm; G andH). Cells in A–F were extracted in 0.01% saponin prior to methanol fixation. PKP-1 or the PKP-1 head domain but not the armadillo repeat domain localized and recruited DP-NTP to cell-cell borders.To define which domain of PKP-1 was responsible for enhancing DP-NTP recruitment to borders, DP-NTP was co-expressed with either the head domain of PKP-1 (Fig. 1, E and F) or with the carboxyl-terminal armadillo repeat region of PKP-1 (Fig. 1,G and H). Similar to full-length PKP-1, the PKP-1 head domain localized at borders and in the nucleus (Fig.1F). The head domain also enhanced DP-NTP recruitment to borders, although to a lesser extent than full-length PKP-1. Both full-length PKP-1 and the head domain localized to cell-cell borders even when expressed in the absence of DP-NTP or exogenously expressed cadherins (not shown). The PKP-1 armadillo domain did not enhance DP-NTP recruitment to borders, and both DP-NTP (Fig. 1G) and the PKP-1 armadillo domain exhibited a cytoplasmic distribution. These data indicate that PKP-1 enhances DP-NTP recruitment to cell borders and that this activity is contained within the amino-terminal head domain of PKP-1. Furthermore, this activity does not require co-expression of exogenous desmosomal cadherins.PKP-1 Co-immunoprecipitates with DP-NTP and the PKP-1 Head Domain Binds to the Amino-terminal Domain of DesmoplakinTo establish the hierarchy of protein-protein interactions in which PKP-1 participates, we addressed first whether PKP-1, like plakoglobin, interacts with desmosomal cadherins and second whether PKP-1 interacts with the amino-terminal domain of desmoplakin. PKP-1 was co-expressed in COS cells with the desmosomal cadherin Dsg1 (Fig.2) or with DP-NTP (Fig.3). As reported previously (27, 30), Dsg1 and plakoglobin form complexes as demonstrated by the presence of Dsg1 in the plakoglobin immunoprecipitation (Fig. 2A). In contrast, Dsg1 was not detected when PKP-1 was immunoprecipitated in parallel experiments (Fig. 2B). Furthermore, PKP-1 did not co-immunoprecipitate with Dsg1 when antibodies directed against the Dsg1 extracellular domain were used (not shown). Similar results were obtained when Dsc2a was tested for complex formation with PKP-1 (not shown).Download: Download full-size imageFigure 2. Dsg1 co-immunoprecipitates with plakoglobin but not PKP-1 . Dsg1 was transiently expressed in COS cells alone or in the presence of either plakoglobin or PKP-1. In cells co-expressing plakoglobin and Dsg1 (A), plakoglobin antibodies co-immunoprecipitated (IP) Myc-tagged Dsg1. In contrast, an antibody directed against the PKP-1 head immunoprecipitated PKP-1 but not Dsg1 (B). Note that COS cells express some endogenous plakoglobin. The asterisk inB identifies PKP-1. The 51-kDa bands represent IgG.Download: Download full-size imageFigure 3. PKP-1 forms complexes with the amino-terminal domain of desmoplakin. DP-NTP was transiently expressed in COS cells either alone or in the presence of PKP-1. M2 antibody-coupled beads were used to immunoprecipitate FLAG-tagged DP-NTP and associated proteins. Immunoblot analysis was carried out using antibodies directed against PKP-1 or DP-NTP. PKP-1 co-immunoprecipitated (IP) with DP-NTP (70 kDa) and was not precipitated by M2 antibody-agarose beads in the absence of DP-NTP.Similar to previous results with plakoglobin, PKP-1 co-immunoprecipitated with DP-NTP (Fig. 3). To determine whether PKP-1 binds directly to DP-NTP or to the desmosomal cadherins, yeast two-hybrid analysis was carried out. The PKP-1 head domain and armadillo domains were tested for interactions with DP-NTP, the Dsg1 cytoplasmic domain, and the Dsc2a cytoplasmic domain. Consistent with the co-immunoprecipitation analysis, the PKP-1 head domain interacted strongly with DP-NTP as determined by a β-galactosidase reporter assay (Fig. 4). The PKP-1 head domain also interacted with the Dsg1 cytoplasmic tail in this assay, but a significant interaction with the Dsc2a cytoplasmic domain was not detected. The PKP-1 armadillo repeat domain did not bind to either DP-NTP or to the desmosomal cadherin cytoplasmic tail domains. This is in contrast to the armadillo repeat domain of plakoglobin, which does bind to DP-NTP (8, 23). Similar results were obtained using growth in the absence of histidine as the reporter for protein interactions (not shown).Download: Download full-size imageFigure 4. DP-NTP binds directly to the PKP-1 head domain. Yeast two-hybrid analysis was used to define domains of PKP-1 that interact with DP-NTP using a β-galactosidase assay and the substrate 4-methylumbelliferyl β-d-galactopyranoside (MUG) as a reporter assay for protein interactions. The PKP-1 head domain and armadillo repeat domain (Arm) were tested for interactions with DP-NTP, the cytoplasmic tail of desmoglein-1 (Dsg1), or the cytoplasmic tail of desmocollin-2a (Dsc2). Interactions between p53 and large T antigen (LgT) are shown as a positive control. The head domain of PKP-1 binds directly to the amino-terminal domain of DP-NTP. As reported for full-length PKP-1 (10), the PKP-1 head domain also interacts with Dsg1, although this interaction was not detected in immunoprecipitates from cell lysates (Fig. 2). For this representative experiment, each bar represents the average of quadruplicate measurements for an independent clone.DISCUSSIONThe results presented here provide insights into both the molecular basis of a cutaneous disorder in patients lacking PKP-1 (16) and into the role of PKP-1 in desmosome assembly. In addition to binding to keratins (10, 17, 19), PKP-1 may also facilitate intermediate filament attachment to the desmosomal plaque by enhancing desmoplakin recruitment to the desmosome. In patients lacking PKP-1, epidermal fragility and blistering would be predicted because of the loss of intermediate filament-binding proteins in the desmosome. The head domain of PKP-1 but not the armadillo repeat domain binds to and recruits desmoplakin to cell borders (Figs. 1 and 4), highlighting a fundamental difference between PKP-1 and plakoglobin. In the case of plakoglobin, desmoplakin binds directly to the central armadillo motifs, and, although the first three repeats retain some binding ability, the entire collection of 13 repeats is required for a robust interaction (not shown). The fact that the PKP-1 armadillo domain remained diffuse in the cytoplasm was somewhat surprising because the arm repeats of plakoglobin, β-catenin, p120, and p00713 all bind to cadherins (31). PKP-1 does bind to some desmosomal cadherins when tested by in vitro overlay assays4(10, 32), and PKP-1 did interact with Dsg1 in the yeast two-hybrid assay. However, the interaction was between Dsg1 and the non-armadillo head domain of PKP-1 (Fig. 4). Furthermore, in contrast to plakoglobin (8, 23), transfection experiments demonstrated that full-length PKP-1 does not require co-expression with a cadherin to localize and recruit DP-NTP to cell-cell borders (Fig. 1). It is possible that PKP-1 preferentially associates with certain isoforms of desmosomal cadherins that are co-expressed with PKP-1 during epidermal differentiation, such as Dsg1 and or Dsc1. However, it appears that the primary binding partner for PKP-1 is desmoplakin and that equimolar amounts of cadherin·PKP-1 are not required for PKP-1 assembly into the plaque.Previous studies suggest that lateral interactions among desmosomal components are critical to the assembly process (8, 10). Together with the data presented here showing that PKP-1 enhances desmoplakin recruitment to the plasma membrane, these observations are consistent with the model in Fig. 5. In the absence of PKP-1, the number of available desmosomal cadherin-plakoglobin complexes would limit the total amount of desmoplakin present at the junction. However, the presence of PKP-1 would overcome this limitation by providing additional desmoplakin-binding sites at the membrane. Consistent with this, increased desmosomal localization of endogenous desmoplakin was observed in COS cells transiently expressing PKP-1 (not shown). The model also predicts that PKP-1 could associate laterally with multiple desmoplakin molecules, which might occur if PKP-1 forms dimers or multimers or if each PKP-1 molecule has multiple desmoplakin-binding sites. Because our present data cannot provide quantitative information on the stoichiometry of PKP-1·DP complexes, future work will be needed to test these possibilities. However, if PKP-1 were to associate with at least two desmoplakin molecules, this would provide an explanation for its ability to enhance DP-NTP recruitment to cell borders in the absence of exogenously expressed cadherins and plakoglobin. Secondary interactions between PKP-1 and the desmosomal cadherins might also occur, leading to further strengthening of the adhesive complex (see also Ref. 10).Download: Download full-size imageFigure 5. A model for desmosome assembly. In the presence of PKP-1, there is an increase in desmoplakin (DP) recruitment and enhanced intermediate filament attachment. In the absence of PKP-1, the number of available cadherin-plakoglobin (PG) complexes would limit desmoplakin accumulation at the membrane. The schematic summarizes current information regarding the hierarchy of interactions among desmosomal components; however, a determination of the absolute stoichiometry of these interactions awaits future study.The data presented in this study also suggest that plakoglobin and PKP-1 exhibit fundamentally different modes of assembly into the desmosomal plaque, with plakoglobin linking desmosomal cadherins to desmoplakin and PKP-1 functioning largely in lateral interactions. Consistent with this hypothesis is the observation that desmosomes in suprabasal layers of the epidermis are larger than simple epithelial desmosomes or desmosomes from basal cells. During epidermal differentiation, desmosomes may increase in size and stability because of insertion of PKP-1/DP-complexes, thereby enhancing desmosome interactions with the cytoskeleton and rendering cells more resistant to mechanical stress. Presumably, this architectural arrangement of both linear and lateral interactions provides for a strong adhesive junction with multiple protein-protein interactions as targets for cellular regulation.AcknowledgmentsWe thank Drs. Chem., 269 (1994), pp. 14075-14080View PDFView articleView in ScopusGoogle ScholarCited by (127)Desmosome structure, composition and function2008, Biochimica et Biophysica Acta - BiomembranesCitation Excerpt :In this chain plakoglobin may act as a linker between the desmosomal cadherins and desmoplakin, or it may be that the desmosomal cadherins interact directly with desmoplakin [67,71] and that plakoglobin is involved in regulating lateral interactions and desmosome size (see above). Plakophilins interact with multiple partners (desmosomal cadherins, plakoglobin, desmoplakin and intermediate filament proteins) and could also act as linkers or be involved in lateral interactions [72]. A number of studies have suggested that the head domain of plakophilins is sufficient for plasma membrane localisation and is required for the subsequent recruitment of desmoplakin [72,73].Show abstractDesmosomes are intercellular junctions of epithelia and cardiac muscle. They resist mechanical stress because they adopt a strongly adhesive state in which they are said to be hyper-adhesive and which distinguishes them from other intercellular junctions; desmosomes are specialised for strong adhesion and their failure can result in diseases of the skin and heart. They are also dynamic structures whose adhesiveness can switch between high and low affinity adhesive states during processes such as embryonic development and wound healing, the switching being signalled by protein kinase C. Desmosomes may also act as signalling centres, regulating the availability of signalling molecules and thereby participating in fundamental processes such as cell proliferation, differentiation and morphogenesis. Here we consider the structure, composition and function of desmosomes, and their role in embryonic development and disease.Connexin43 remodeling caused by inhibition of plakophilin-2 expression in cardiac cells2007, Circulation ResearchRequirement of plakophilin 2 for heart morphogenesis and cardiac junction formation2004, Journal of Cell BiologyWorking out the strength and flexibility of desmosomes2004, Nature Reviews Molecular Cell BiologyAre desmosomes more than tethers for intermediate filaments?2000, Nature Reviews Molecular Cell BiologyEpithelial structural proteins of the skin and oral cavity: Function in health and disease2000, Critical Reviews in Oral Biology and MedicineView all citing articles on Scopus*This work was supported by March of Dimes Grant FY98–0073, and by National Institutes of Health Grants RO1AR43380 and PO1DE12328 (to K.                         Share IconShareFacebookTwitterLinkedInEmailTools IconToolsGet PermissionsCite IconCiteSearch SiteCitationYasushi Hanakawa, Masayuki Amagai, Yuji Shirakata, Koji Sayama, Koji Hashimoto; Different effects of dominant negative mutants of desmocollin and desmoglein on the cell-cell adhesion of keratinocytes. J Cell Sci 15 May 2000; 113 (10): 1803–1811. doi: https://doi.org/10.1242/jcs.113.10.1803Download citation file:Ris (Zotero)Reference ManagerEasyBibBookendsMendeleyPapersEndNoteRefWorksBibTextoolbar searchSearch Dropdown Menutoolbar searchsearch inputSearch input auto suggestfilter your searchAll contentAll journalsJournal of Cell ScienceSearchAdvanced SearchABSTRACTDesmosomes contain two types of cadherin: desmocollin (Dsc) and desmoglein (Dsg). In this study, we examined the different roles that Dsc and Dsg play in the formation of desmosomes, by using dominant-negative mutants. We constructed recombinant adenoviruses (Ad) containing truncated mutants of E-cadherin, desmocollin 3a, and desmoglein 3 lacking a large part of their extracellular domains (EcadΔEC, Dsc3aΔEC, Dsg3ΔEC), using the Cre-loxP Ad system to circumvent the problem of the toxicity of the mutants to virus-producing cells. When Dsc3aΔEC Ad-infected HaCaT cells were cultured with high levels of calcium, E-cadherin and β-catenin, which are marker molecules for the adherens junction, disappeared from the cell-cell contact sites, and cell-cell adhesion was disrupted. This also occurred in the cells infected with EcadΔEC Ad. With Dsg3ΔEC Ad infection, keratin insertion at the cell-cell contact sites was inhibited and desmoplakin, a marker of desmosomes, was stained in perinuclear dots while the adherens junctions remained intact. Dsc3aΔEC Ad inhibited the induction of adherens junctions and the subsequent formation of desmosomes with the calcium shift, while Dsg3ΔEC Ad only inhibited the formation of desmosomes. To further determine whether Dsc3aΔEC directly affected adherens junctions, mouse fibroblast L cells transfected with E-cadherin (LEC5) were infected with these mutant Ads. Both Dsc3aΔEC and EcadΔEC inhibited the cell-cell adhesion of LEC5 cells, as determined by the cell aggregation assay, while Dsg3ΔEC did not. These results indicate that the dominant negative effects of Dsg3ΔEC were restricted to desmosomes, while those of Dsc3aΔEC were observed in both desmosomes and adherens junctions. Furthermore, the cytoplasmic domain of Dsc3aΔEC coprecipitated both plakoglobin and β-catenin in HaCaT cells. In addition, β-catenin was found to bind the endogenous Dsc in HaCaT cells. These findings lead us to speculate that Dsc interacts with components of the adherens junctions through β-catenin, and plays a role in nucleating desmosomes after the adherens junctions have been established.Keywords:Desmosome,Adherens junction,Desmocollin,Desmoglein,E-CadherinINTRODUCTIONCell-cell adhesion is considered important in the development and maintenance of organ tissue (Takeichi, 1995; Gumbiner, 1996; Steinberg, 1996). In squamous cell epithelium, cell adhesion provides tissue integrity to overcome the outer environment. Epidermis cell adhesion is maintained by two major adhesion structures: adherens junctions and desmosomes. Adherens junctions are composed of classic cadherins and the cytoplasmic plaque proteins α- and β-catenin and plakoglobin, and are connected to actin microfilaments (Takeichi, 1995). The classic cadherins are a group of calcium-dependent, cell-to-cell adhesion molecules that span the plasma membrane once. Cadherins are thought to mediate homophilic interaction, as suggested by the cell adhesion zipper model (Shapiro et al., 1995). On the other hand, desmosomes are composed of two kinds of desmosomal cadherins: desmoglein (Dsg) and desmocollin (Dsc).Desmosomal cadherins bind to the cytoplasmic plaque proteins plakoglobin and desmoplakin, and are linked to keratin intermediate filaments (Green and Jones, 1996; Amagai, 1996). Several studies have shown that the establishment of adherens junctions is a prerequisite for the formation of desmosomes. Functional inhibition of classic cadherin impairs adherens junctions as well as desmosomes. An antibody neutralizing E-cadherin delayed the Ca2+-induced redistribution of desmoplakin for several hours (Wheelock and Jensen, 1992). The combination of anti-E-cadherin and anti-P-cadherin antibodies inhibited formation of both adherens junctions and desmosomes (Lewis et al., 1994). Both the adherens junctions and desmosomes were disrupted in Pam cells stably expressing a dominant negative mutant of N-cadherin (Amagai et al., 1995). Similarly, normal human keratinocytes transfected with a dominant negative mutant of E-cadherin by retrovirus vector showed disrupted adherens junctions as well as desmosomes (Zhu and Watt, 1996). On the other hand, the rescue of functional adherens junctions led to full development of desmosomes. A lung carcinoma cell line, PC9, which expresses E-cadherin and β-catenin, but no α-catenin, does not form any kind of junction, and proliferates as a loose aggregation in suspension culture. When PC9 cells were transfected with αN-catenin, the transfectants formed adherens junctions as well as desmosomes and tight junctions, thereby proliferating in a firm aggregation (Watabe et al., 1994). All of these findings indicate that the formation of adherens junctions must precede the formation of desmosomes. In this study, we attempted to clarify the different roles of Dsc and Dsg, especially their roles in the assembly of desmosomes. To address this question, we constructed dominant negative mutants of Dsc and Dsg and introduced them into cultured keratinocytes with an adenovirus vector. The effects of the dominant negative mutant of Dsg were restricted to desmosomes, while those of Dsc were found not only in desmosomes, but also in adherens junctions. Furthermore, the cytoplasmic domain of the Dsc mutant and the wild-type Dsc were found to bind β-catenin, which is not found in desmosomes. This result suggests that Dsc may be a key molecule for initiating desmosome formation after the establishment of adherens junctions at cell-cell contact sites.MATERIALS AND METHODSCell cultureThe human embryonic kidney cell line 293 was obtained from American Type Tissue Culture (ATCC; Rockville, MD). The human naturally immortalized keratinocyte HaCaT cell line was a kind gift from Dr Norbert Fusenig (German Cancer Research Center, Heidelberg, Germany). LEC5 cells are a stable transformant of the mouse fibroblast L cells that express E-cadherin (Amagai et al., 1994). These cells were cultured in Dulbecco’s modification of Eagle’s medium (DMEM) with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS).To prepare a low-calcium medium, calcium free DMEM (Gibco BRL, Gainsburg, MD) was supplemented with 10% FBS that was treated with 10% Chelex 100 (Bio-Rad, Hercules, CA) to deplete calcium, and then CaCl2 was added to a final concentration of 0.05 mM. For the calcium shift assay, the same number of cells was inoculated after trypsinization, and maintained in the low-calcium medium overnight on plastic culture slides (Nalge-Nunc, Napierville, IL). Then CaCl2 was added at a final concentration of 1.5 mM and the cells were incubated for the indicated periods.Plasmid constructionThe plasmid containing the full-length cDNA encoding mouse E-cadherin (pBATEM2) was a kind gift from Dr Masatoshi Takeichi (Kyoto University, Japan). The full-length cDNA encoding human desmocollin 3a was a kind gift from Dr Kazuo Kawamura (Institute of Cytosignal Research, and Kirin Beer Co., Japan). cDNA for desmoglein 3 was described previously (Amagai et al., 1991). Mutants of E-cadherin, desmocollin 3a, and desmoglein 3 (called EcadΔEC, DscΔEC, and DsgΔEC, respectively) were constructed by deleting a large part of the extracellular domain and flanking the C-terminal end with a seven-c-myc tag. EcadΔEC (nucleotides 9-578, 1854-2721) was generated by PCR using primers ECF15’ (5’-GAAGATCTACC-CGGCCCTGCCCGACC-3’, BglII site at the 5’ end) and ECF13’ (5’-GGGGTACCCTTTTCATTTTCGGGGC-3’, KpnI site at the 3’ end), ECF25’ (5’-GGGGTACCATCCCAGAACCTCGAAAC-3’, KpnI site at the 5’ end) and ECF23’ (5’-CGGAATTCGTCGTCGCCACCGCC-3’, EcoRI site at the 3’ end). The two E-cad fragments produced by PCR were subcloned into pcDNA1-7myc/Amp (pcEcadΔEC). pcDNA1-7myc/Amp was a kind gift from Dr Kathleen Green (Northwestern University, Chicago, IL; Roth et al., 1991).Dsc3aΔEC (nucleotides 1-481, 1819-2751) was generated by PCR using primers DCF15’ (5’-CGGGATCCCTCTAAAAGCTGCTG-CAG-3’, BamHI site at the 5’ end) DCF13’ (5’-GGGGTACCCATA-GAGCAAGGAATAGG-3’, KpnI site at the 3’ end), DCF25’ (5’-GGG-GTACCTGCAAACCAAAAATGGGG-3’, KpnI site at the 5’ end), and DCF23’ (5’-CGGAATTCCTTTGTGCATGCTTCTGC-3’, EcoRI site at the 3’ end). The PCR products were subcloned into pcDNA1-7myc/Amp (pcDsc3aΔEC).Dsg3ΔEC (nucleotides 9-272, 1563-3080) was generated by PCR using primers DGF15’ (5’-GAAGATCTAACTGCAGACGGCT-GGC3’ BamHI site at the 5’ end), DGF13’ (5’GGGGTACCATCTTC-TCCTTCTCTGC-3’, KpnI site at the 3’ end), DGF25’ (5’-GGGGTA-CCACAGCTGTCCTCGAAAAAGATG-3’, KpnI site at the 5’ end), and DGF23’ (5’-CGGAATTCTATTAGACGGGAGCAAGG-3’, Eco-RI site at the 3’ end). The PCR products were subcloned into pcDNA1-7myc/Amp (pcDsg3ΔEC).Adenovirus vector construction and infectionThe cosmid cassette pAxCALNLw (Kanegae et al., 1996), loxP-NeoR-loxP unit under a CA promoter consisting of a cytomegalovirus enhancer and chicken β-actin promoter (Niwa et al., 1991), nuclear localizing signal-tagged Cre recombinase-expressing Ad (AxCANCre), control Ad Ax1w, and the parent virus Ad5-dlX (Miyake et al., 1996) were all kind gifts from Dr Izumi Saito (Tokyo University, Japan). Fragments of EcadΔEC, Dsg3ΔEC, and Dsc3aΔEC were subcloned into the Ad cosmid cassette pAxCALNLw. Ad containing CALNL and EcadΔEC, Dsg3ΔEC, or Dsc3aΔEC (AxCALNLEcadΔEC, AxCALNLDsg3ΔEC, AxCALNLDsc3aΔEC, respectively) were generated by the COS-TPC method (Miyake et al., 1996). The cosmid DNA was mixed with the EcoT22I-digested DNA-terminal protein complex of Ad5-dlX, and used to cotransfect 293 cells. Recombinant viruses were generated through homologous recombination in 293 cells. Virus stocks were prepared by a standard procedure (Miyake et al., 1996). Concentrated, purified virus stocks were prepared by the CsCl gradient method and the virus titer was checked with the plaque formation assay. HaCaT cells were doubly infected with AxCANCre and Ax1w, AxCALNLEcadΔEC, AxCALNLDsg3ΔEC, or AxCALNLDsc3a-ΔEC. HaCaT cells were infected with AxCANCre at a multiplicity of infection (MOI) of 15 and Ax1w, AxCALNLEcadΔEC, AxCALNL-Dsg3ΔEC, or AxCALNLDsc3aΔEC at an MOI of 15 (Cre: mutant = 1:1). LEC5 cells were doubly infected at an MOI of 100 (50+50).AntibodiesThe following monoclonal antibodies were used: AE1 and AE3 (mouse anti-keratin intermediate filament, PROGEN, Heidelberg, Germany), 9E10.2 (mouse anti-myc, ATCC), anti-β-catenin (mouse, Transduction Laboratories, Lexington, Kentucky), DPI/II (mouse anti-desmoplakin, PROGEN), PG5.1 (mouse anti-plakoglobin, PROGEN), 6H6 (mouse anti-Dsg3, C. Proby et al., unpublished), HECD-1 (mouse anti-E-cadherin, Takara, Japan), 52-3D (mouse anti-desmocollin, a kind gift from Dr David Garrod, Manchester University, UK), and Dsc-U114 (mouse anti-desmocollin3, PROGEN). The following rabbit antisera were used: Z622 (anti-pan-keratin, DAKO, Copenhagen, Denmark), anti-myc (a kind gift from Dr John Stanley, Pennsylvania University) and anti-KK5 (anti-desmocollin3 antibody, a kind gift from Dr Kazuo Kawamura).Fluorescein isothiocyanate (FITC)-conjugated goat anti-mouse or goat anti-rabbit antibody (Kirkegaard and Perry Laboratories; KPL, Gaithersburg, MD) and rhodamine-conjugated goat anti-rabbit antibody (BIOSOURCE, Camarillo, CA) were used.ImmunohistochemistryCells grown on Lab-Tech 4-well culture slides (Nalge-Nunc, Napierville, IL) were fixed with methanol at –20°C for 20 minutes and permeabilized with 0.05% Triton X-100 in Tris-buffered saline containing 1 mM CaCl2 (TBS-Ca2+) at room temperature (RT) for 5 minutes. After incubation with 1% bovine serum albumin (BSA) in TBS-Ca2+ for 20 minutes at RT, the cells were incubated with various antibodies at the appropriate dilution in 1% BSA in TBS-Ca2+ for 1 hour at RT. The samples were further incubated with FITC- or rhodamine-conjugated second antibody at the appropriate dilution in 1% BSA in TBS-Ca2+ for 1 hour at RT.Immunoblotting and immunoprecipitationFor immunoblotting, cells were lysed in sodium dodecylsulfate (SDS) sample buffer (62.5 mM Tris-HCl, pH 7.5, 1% SDS, 0.0025% bromophenol blue, 10% glycerol, 2.5% 2-mercaptoethanol) and subjected to immunoblotting using enhanced chemifluorescence according to the manufacturer’s protocol (Amersham Pharmacia Biotech; APB, Uppsala, Sweden). For soluble and insoluble fractionation, the cells were scraped in 1% Nonidet P-40 and1% Triton X-100 in TBS-Ca on ice. After centrifuging at 15,000 rpm for 10 minutes at 4°C, the supernatant was collected as the soluble fraction. The pellet was dissolved in SDS sample buffer as the insoluble fraction. For immunoprecipitation, Ad-infected cells were extracted with 1% Nonidet P-40, 1% Triton X-100, 2 mM CaCl2, and 150 mM NaCl in 10 mM Tris-HCl, pH 7.4, with protease inhibitors (aprotinin 2 μg/ml, leupeptin 2 μg/ml, PMSF 1 mM). Aliquots of cell lysate were preadsorbed with normal mouse IgG or normal rabbit IgG and Protein G-Sepharose (APB), then precipitated with various antibodies and Protein G-Sepharose. Immunoprecipitates were eluted from Protein G-Sepharose with SDS sample buffer and subjected to immunoblotting. The immunoblots were analyzed by using ImageQuantTM (Amersham Pharmacia Biotech) software to determine the relative ratio in the immunoprecipitated complex.Aggregation assaySingle cell suspensions of Ad-infected LEC5 were obtained with 1 mM ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) in 10 mM Hepes-buffered calcium and magnesium free Hanks’ balanced salt solution (Gibco-BRL). The cells were then washed twice in Hepes-buffered Hanks’ solution with 10 μg/ml deoxyribonuclease I and 10% FBS in the first wash. The cells were resuspended in Hepes-buffered Hanks’ solution with 10 μg/ml deoxyribonuclease I and 1 mM CaCl2. Approximately 5×105 cells per 2.5 ml were incubated in 35-mm dishes (precoated with 1% bovine serum albumin at 37°C for 2 hours) with gentle shaking at 37°C for 1 hour, then incubated at room temperature without shaking for 1 hour. The average projected area of the aggregates was quantified using NIH image software.RESULTSConstruction of Ad containing EcadΔEC, Dsc3aΔEC, and Dsg3ΔEC using the Cre-loxP systemMutants of E-cadherin, desmocollin 3, and desmoglein 3 were constructed by deleting a large part of the extracellular domain, and flanked with a seven-c-myc tag (EcadΔEC, Dsc3aΔEC, and Dsg3ΔEC, respectively; Fig. 1). All three mutants were designed to conserve signal peptides, prosequences, extracellular anchor domain, the transmembrane domain, and the entire cytoplasmic domain. Initially, we failed to obtain Ad that expressed these truncated mutants, probably because the truncated molecules were toxic to 293 cells, which were used to produce the recombinant virus. Therefore, to prevent the expression of the truncated products during production of the recombinant virus, loxP flanking a stuffer sequence, consisting of a neomycin-resistant gene, was interposed between the CAG promoter and the coding regions for the mutants (Kanegae et al., 1996). Co-infection with Ad expressing Cre recombinase removed the stuffer sequence and turned on the expression of the mutant cadherins. The expression of mutant proteins was detected 6 hours after infection and reached a plateau at from 24 to 36 hours (Fig. 2A,B,C,D). The three mutants were all 7-myc tagged and we were able to compare the relative expression level of each mutant. The levels were essentially the same. The exogenous expression of these mutants did not alter the endogenous expression of plakoglobin, Dsg3, Dsc, or E-cadherin. Almost 100% of cells expressed the mutant molecules when HaCaT cells were coinfected with Ad for the mutant cadherins and Cre recombinase flanked with the nuclear localization signal (NCre) at a multiplicity of infection (MOI) of 30 (mutant: Cre=1:1; Fig. 3E,F,G,H). No apparent toxic effect was seen in the cells infected with control Ad (Ax1w) and NCre Ad at an MOI of 30.Fig. 1.View largeDownload slideConstruction of mutant cDNAs. One possible mechanism for the blocking effect of Dsc3aΔEC on adherens junction formation might be the sequestration of β-catenin from E-cadherin by Dsc3aΔEC.DISCUSSIONTo investigate the mechanisms of desmosomal assembly and the different roles of Dsc and Dsg, we constructed dominant negative mutants of three different cadherins: E-cadherin, desmocollin, and desmoglein (EcadΔEC, Dsc3aΔEC, and Dsg3ΔEC, respectively). EcadΔEC blocked the formation of adherens junctions and the subsequent assembly of desmosomes, which is consistent with previous findings (Zhu and Watt, 1996; Amagai et al., 1995). Dsg3ΔEC inhibited the formation of desmosomes, but had no apparent effects on adherens junctions. In marked contrast with Dsg3ΔEC, Dsc3aΔEC affected not only desmosomes, but also adherens junctions. These different effects of the cadherin mutants were confirmed in three different situations: in stable cell-cell junctions using HaCaT cells cultured in the high Ca2+ condition, during the induction phase of cell-cell junctions using HaCaT cells with a Ca2+ shift, and on adherens junctions using L cells transfected with E-cadherin. These findings indicate that the dominant negative effect of the Dsg mutant was limited to desmosomes, while that of the Dsc mutant was extended to adherens junctions. Furthermore, we demonstrated that these cadherin mutants were actually found in the insoluble fractions, suggesting that these mutants were integrated in junction complexes. Therefore, it is speculated that the dominant-negative effects are caused by direct interaction between the mutants and endogenous components of adherens junctions or desmosomes.Then, why was the effect of the Dsc mutant extended to adherens junctions, while that of Dsg was limited to desmosomes? Since the establishment of adherens junctions is a prerequisite for the formation of desmosomes and Dsc3aΔEC had the same effect on LEC5 cells, which do not have desmosomes, these findings suggest that Dsc may exert its effect on adherens junctions by interacting with a component(s) of adherens junctions. There could be two distinct groups of components: molecules interacting laterally through the extracellular domain or transmembrane domain and molecules interacting through the cytoplasmic domain.By combining immunoprecipitation with subsequent immunoblotting, we found that the cytoplasmic domain of Dsc3aΔEC interacted not only with plakoglobin, but also with β-catenin (Fig. 8). A number of studies have shown that plakoglobin is found in both desmosomes and adherens junctions, while β-catenin is found only in adherens junctions (Ozawa and Kemler, 1992; Kowalczyk et al., 1994; Plott et al., 1994; Jou et al., 1995). Under certain conditions, however, β-catenin will bind to Dsg. In A431 cells that overexpress exogenous full-length Dsg1, β-catenin formed a complex with Dsg1 (Norvell and Green, 1998). In plakoglobin null-mutant mice, β-catenin became localized in desmosomes and coprecipitated with Dsg (Bierkamp et al., 1999). Unfortunately, the interaction between β-catenin and Dsc was not fully investigated in these systems. In our system, we did not detect an association between Dsg3ΔEC and β-catenin, but did detect one between Dsc3aΔEC and β-catenin. This interaction was found in two different conditions; in Dsc3aΔEC-infected HaCaT cells and in Dsc3aΔEC-infected LEC5 cells (Fig. 8). Furthermore, β-catenin was found to bind the endogenous Dsc in HaCaT cells (Fig. 9), suggesting that Dsc may have an inherent property of binding to β-catenin. Thus, one possible mechanism of the dominant-negative effect of Dsc3aΔEC on adherens junctions is that it sequesters β-catenin away from the endogenous E-cadherin. This speculation is also supported by the finding that the dominant negative effects are no longer observed once the catenin binding domain is deleted from the mutants (Nieman et al., 1999; Zhu and Watt, 1996).HaCaT cells express Dsg2, Dsg3, Dsc2, and Dsc3, but not Dsg1 or Dsc1 (Schmidt et al., 1994); However, the relative level of expression of each isotype is not known. When we compared the binding capacity based on the results of immunoprecipitation (Fig. 8), EcadΔEC bound approximately six times more β-catenin than Dsc3aΔEC did, which is consistent with the dominant-negative effects on adherens junctions being stronger in EcadΔEC than in Dsc3aΔEC. However, the level of Dsc3aΔEC expression was only one and a half times higher than that of the wild-type Dsc3a (data not shown), which makes it difficult to imagine that Dsc3aΔEC could produce such effects. Quantification of the amount of plakoglobin complexed with mutants revealed that Dsg3ΔEC, Dsc3aΔEC, and EcadΔEC were expressed in a ratio of approximately 2:1:3, respectively. It is previously reported that plakoglobin:Dsc2a complex exhibited an 1:1 and plakoglobin:Dsg1 exhibited an 6:1 or 7:1 (Kowalczyck et al., 1996; Witcher et al., 1996). Because Dsg3ΔEC is a mutant derived from Dsg3, there is a possibility that Dsg1 and Dsg3 possess different binding capacity for plakoglobin. However, these assumptions are based on the findings for the soluble fractions. We do not have any good way to examine the molecular ratio in the insoluble fractions, which represent the actual integrated molecules in established junctions.Another possible mechanism of the dominant negative effects of these mutants is inhibition of the endogenous cadherins by lateral interaction through the extracellular domain or transmembrane domain. However, we could not detect any binding of mutants to endogenous cadherins (data not shown). This negative finding does not necessarily exclude the possibility that mutants might form a lateral complex with endogenous cadherins, which might be found only in the insoluble fraction.Dsc plays an important role in initiating desmosomal assembly. Desmosome formation of MDCK cells was blocked by specific Fab’ against Dsc in high Ca2+ conditions (Cowin et al., 1984). In low Ca2+ conditions, Dsc was distributed over the entire cell surface, while Dsg, plakoglobin, and desmoplakin were located throughout the cytoplasm (Watt et al., 1984). A chimeric protein consisting of the transmembrane region of connexin 32, a gap junction protein, and the Dsc1a cytoplasmic domain formed a new gap junction, to which desmoplakin and plakoglobin were recruited and keratin intermediate filaments were inserted (Troyanovsky et al., 1993). These findings indicate that Dsc has a key role in initiating desmosomal assembly, and that the cytoplasmic tail of Dsc has a signal sufficient to recruit plakoglobin, desmoplakin, and keratin insertions.There are two models for the molecular mechanism of desmosomal assembly. In one, desmosomes are pre-assembled in the cytoplasmic vesicles and transferred as a unit to the plasma membrane (Duden and Franke, 1988; Demlehner et al., 1995). In the other, free Dsc or Dsg exist diffusely on the cell membrane and trigger the recruitment of other desmosomal components on the membrane (Watt et al., 1984; Jones and Goldman, 1985; Pasdar et al., 1991). In support of the first model, using electron microscopy, Demlehner et al. (1995) found a pre-assembled unit (half-desmosome) that was composed of Dsg, Dsc, plakoglobin, and desmoplakin, and was often attached to keratin filaments; they proposed that this pre-assembled desmosome is a precursor of mature desmosomes. In support of the second model, adherens junctions form the initial cell-cell contacts, and subsequently Dsc and Dsg accumulate at the contact sites and the inner plaque proteins, plakoglobin and desmoplakin, are assorted to link keratin filaments. In the low Ca2+ condition, Dsg and desmoplakin are not associated with each other. Dsc, Dsg, plakoglobin, and desmoplakin accumulate at the cell-cell margin and form desmosomes only after the Ca2+ switch (Watt et al., 1984; Jones and Goldman, 1985; Pasdar et al., 1991).Combining our results with previous findings, we propose a hypothesis for the molecular mechanism for desmosome assembly. The initial cell-cell contacts are mediated by classic cadherins, which establish adherens junctions. To produce more stable cell-cell adhesion, Dsc is recruited as an initial component of desmosomes to cell-cell contact sites mediated by adherens junctions. This recruitment may be facilitated by interaction with β-catenin. Once Dsc settles on the cell-cell contact sites, it recruits other desmosomal components, including plakoglobin and desmoplakin, to assemble desmosomes. Thus, Dsc may play an important role in nucleating desmosome formation after the adherens junction is established. Further experiments are required to prove this model of desmosome assembly.ACKNOWLEDGEMENTSWe thank Dr Izumi Saitou (Tokyo, Japan) for the adenovirus expression system and adenovirus Cre-loxP system.                     Coexpression of both types of desmosomal cadherin and plakoglobin confers strong intercellular adhesion
Cristiana Marcozzi,
    Cristiana Marcozzi

                        Share IconShareFacebookTwitterLinkedInEmailTools IconToolsGet PermissionsCite IconCiteSearch SiteCitationCristiana Marcozzi, Ian D. J. Burdett, Roger S. Buxton, Anthony I. Magee; Coexpression of both types of desmosomal cadherin and plakoglobin confers strong intercellular adhesion. J Cell Sci 15 February 1998; 111 (4): 495–509. doi: https://doi.org/10.1242/jcs.111.4.495Download citation file:Ris (Zotero)Reference ManagerEasyBibBookendsMendeleyPapersEndNoteRefWorksBibTextoolbar searchSearch Dropdown Menutoolbar searchsearch inputSearch input auto suggestfilter your searchAll contentAll journalsJournal of Cell ScienceSearchAdvanced SearchABSTRACTDesmosomes are unique intercellular junctions in that they invariably contain two types of transmembrane cadherin molecule, desmocollins and desmogleins. In addition they possess a distinct cytoplasmic plaque structure containing a few major proteins including desmoplakins and the armadillo family member plakoglobin. Desmosomal cadherins are putative cell-cell adhesion molecules and we have tested their adhesive capacity using a transfection approach in mouse L cells. We find that L cells expressing either one or both of the desmosomal cadherins desmocollin 2a or desmoglein 1 display weak cell-cell adhesion activity that is Ca2+-dependent. Both homophilic and heterophilic adhesion could be detected. However, co-expression of plakoglobin with both desmosomal cadherins, but not with desmoglein 1 alone, resulted in a dramatic potentiation of cell-cell aggregation and the accumulation of detergent-insoluble desmosomal proteins at points of cell-cell contact. The effect of plakoglobin seems to be due directly to its interaction with the desmosomal cadherins rather than to its signalling function. The data suggest that the desmosome may obligatorily contain two cadherins and is consistent with a model in which desmocollins and desmogleins may form side by side heterodimers in contrast to the classical cadherins that are homodimeric. Plakoglobin may function by potentiating dimer formation, accretion of dimers to cell-cell contact sites or desmosomal cadherin stability.Keywords:Desmosome,Cadherin,Plakoglobin,AdhesionINTRODUCTIONThe desmosome is a major cell adhesive structure prominent in epithelia, heart muscle and the meninges of the brain and is particularly abundant in stratifying epithelia subject to mechanical stress such as epidermis (Legan et al., 1992). Desmosomes are punctate cell-cell contacts which interact on their cytoplasmic sides with intermediate filaments (e.g. keratins in epithelia, desmin in heart), thus mechanically integrating the cells in the tissue. As well as their role in tissue maintenance, evidence is accumulating that desmosomes or some of their components play an important part in tissue specification and establishment during embryogenesis (Garrod and Fleming, 1990; Cowin and Burke, 1996).Desmosomes contain two types of transmembrane glycoproteins as their putative adhesive components: desmocollins and desmogleins (Buxton et al., 1993). Both of these classes of molecule occur as several different isoforms and are members of the cadherin superfamily (Buxton and Magee, 1992; Magee and Buxton, 1991; Koch and Franke, 1994). These molecules are expressed in tissue- and cell-type specific patterns (Legan et al., 1994; Schmidt et al., 1994). Expression of desmosomal cadherins is differentially regulated during stratification of epidermis in a manner which parallels changes in the adhesive properties of the cells (Arnemann et al., 1993; Legan et al., 1994; Koch and Franke, 1994; Nuber et al., 1995; King et al., 1997).Desmocollins diverge in their overall sequence from classical cadherins and have different cell adhesion recognition sites (Phe/TyrAlaThr/Ser as opposed to HisAlaVal, respectively). There are three known desmocollin genes DSC1, DSC2 and DSC3 which can each give rise to two protein products (designated ‘a’ and ‘b’) by alternative splicing. Three desmogleins are known, Dsg1, Dsg2 and Dsg3, each encoded by separate genes (DSG1, 2 and 3). They have a unique cytoplasmic domain with a 29 amino acid repeat extending beyond the cadherin-homologous region and have the cell adhesion recognition sites Arg/TyrAlaLeu.Classical cadherins have been shown to mediate homophilic Ca2+-dependent cell-cell adhesion by transfection of their cDNAs into mouse L cells that do not normally express cadherins (Nagafuchi et al., 1987; Nose et al., 1988; Edelman et al., 1987). Studies of L cells transfected with E-cadherin cDNAs altered by site-directed mutagenesis of the intracellular region have shown that only those constructs capable of binding to the actin cytoskeleton via catenins function in adhesion (Ozawa et al., 1990; Nagafuchi and Takeichi, 1989).β-Catenin, a member of the armadillo family, binds directly to the C-terminal region of cadherin cytoplasmic domains (Ozawa et al., 1990; Ozawa and Kemler, 1992). α-Catenin, a vinculin-like molecule, binds to β-catenin and mediates interaction with the actin microfilament system. The cytoplasmic tails of desmogleins and desmocollins differ from those of cadherins and interact with intermediate filaments through different linker proteins including the armadillo family member plakoglobin (PG; Mathur et al., 1994; Troyanovsky et al., 1994a,b) and desmoplakins (Stappenbeck and Green, 1992; Stappenbeck et al., 1993; Kouklis et al., 1994). These proteins are absent (desmoplakins) or expressed at only very low levels (PG) in L cells. To test the possible adhesive properties of desmosomal cadherins we stably transfected L cells with cDNAs encoding Dsg1 or Dsc2a either singly or in combination. Cells expressing both Dsg1 and Dsc2a were also transfected with PG cDNA. The desmosomal cadherins derived from the introduced cDNAs were expressed and functional in L cells; they conferred weak aggregating activity when present singly or together. Coexpression of PG, however, led to a dramatic increase in cell adhesion activity to a level comparable with classical cadherins. Adhesion activity was Ca2+-dependent and both homophilic and heterophilic binding between desmocollins and desmogleins could be detected. In the light of the recent determination of cadherin domain three-dimensional structures (Shapiro et al., 1995; Nagar et al., 1996) these data suggest possible models for the organisation of the desmosome.MATERIALS AND METHODSPlasmid constructionOur original full length human DSG1 cDNA (Wheeler et al., 1991a,b) contained ∼120 bp of 5′ untranslated sequence derived from cloning events containing four potential incorrect start codons and one in-frame stop codon upstream of the authentic start codon. Preliminary attempts to express this cDNA were unsuccessful so the DSG1 cDNA was reconstructed by PCR of the 5′ end using the primers RSB26 (5′-GAGTATCATCACCAGTG-3′) and RSB120 (5′-TACCAAGCTTATCCAGCAGAGATG-3′) carrying the restriction site for HindIII on the 5′ end and the start site ATG on the 3′ end, and the original plasmid as template. The PCR product of ∼430 bp was purified by agarose gel electrophoresis followed by GeneClean (Bio 101 Inc.) and cut with HindIII and StuI. This fragment was GeneCleaned and ligated to the rest of the DSG1 sequence in pBluescript cut with HindIII and StuI and gel purified to remove the equivalent 5′-region. After sequencing, the reconstructed region of the DSG1 cDNA was found to be error-free, and the entire DSG1 cDNA was directionally subcloned from pBluescript into the eukaryotic expression vector pcDNAIneo (Invitrogen) using the HindIII and BamHI sites and used for transfection of L cells. This vector carries the neomycin resistance gene as a selectable marker and expresses the inserted gene from the strong constitutive cytomegalovirus promoter. The second vector used was pMSGgpt (Pharmacia), in which the inserted cDNA is under the control of the glucocorticoid-inducible mouse mammary tumor virus promoter. The plasmid contains the E. coli xanthine-guanine phosphoribosyl-transferase (gpt) gene, which provides a marker for selecting stable transfectants in eukaryotic cells. The EcoRI-excised human DSC2a cDNA from L5B3 (Parker et al., 1991) was subcloned into pBluescript. In one orientation the SmaI and XhoI restriction sites were used to subclone directionally into pMSGgpt.Clone pHPG Ca 2.1was a kind gift from W. W. Franke. The full-length human PG cDNA was directionally subcloned from pBluescript into pcDNAIneo using the HindIII site. pHygr, which confers resistance to hygromycin B by transcriptional control from the herpes simplex virus type 1 thymidine kinase gene, was obtained from Dr F. Grosveld and was used as selectable marker in co-transfection with PG-pcDNAIneo. The pZeo vector (Invitrogen) was also used as a co-selectable marker for the preparation of triply transfected cells. Constructs were checked for correct insert orientation by restriction mapping and then maxi preps of the plasmid DNAs were purified by CsCl gradient centrifugation.Transfection of L cellsTo obtain stable L cell transfectants we used a modified calcium-phosphate method (Chen and Okayama, 1987). Exponentially growing cells were trypsinized, seeded in a 10 cm Petri dish, and incubated overnight until ∼80% confluent in 10 ml of growth medium (modified Eagle’s medium MEM F-15 (Gibco) supplemented with 10% foetal calf serum). 20 to 30 μg of plasmid DNA were mixed with 0.5 ml of 0.25 M CaCl2, 0.5 ml of 2× BBS (50 mM BES, 280 mM NaCl, 1.5 mM Na2HPO4, pH 6.95) was added and the mixture was incubated for 10 to 20 minutes at room temperature. The calcium phosphate-DNA suspension (1 ml) was added dropwise to the medium over the cells, and the mixture was swirled gently and incubated for 15 to 24 hours at 35°C under 3% CO2. The medium was then removed and the cells were rinsed twice with growth medium, and incubated in fresh medium for 24 hours at 37°C under 5% CO2. The cells were passaged at an appropriate ratio (>1:10) and incubated overnight before selection for stable transformants in growth medium containing 20 μg/ml of mycophenolic acid (Sigma; for pMSGgpt), 500 μg/ml of geneticin/G418 (Sigma; for pcDNAIneo) or 200 μg/ml of hygromycin B (Boehringer Mannheim; for pHygr) for 3 to 4 weeks. Clones were isolated by ring cloning or limiting dilution and expanded. For co-transfection of PG-pcDNAIneo and pHygr, 20 μg and 2 μg of each plasmid were used respectively. For the derivation of triply transfected cells using Zeocin selection a clone of DSC2a-transfected cells was transfected as above with 10 μg of DSG1-pcDNAIneo and 10 μg of PG-pcDNAIneo as well as 1 μg of pZeo. Cells were selected with 250 μg/ml of Zeocin (Invitrogen) for 14 days.ImmunoblottingTotal cell lysates were prepared in gel loading buffer containing 50 mM dithiothreitol, boiled and separated by SDS-PAGE using 7.5% (or 10% for PG) polyacrylamide gels (Laemmli, 1970). Proteins were transferred to nitrocellulose filters (Sartorius) using a Biometra semi-dry blotter at 1 mA/cm2 of gel for 2 hours. Filters were blocked with 5% (w/v) skimmed milk (Marvel) and then incubated with rabbit antiserum to the extracellular domain of Dsc2 (King et al., 1993), mouse monoclonal antibody DG 3.10 to human Dsg1 (Cymbus Bioscence Limited) or rabbit antibody to a recombinant glutathione S-transferase fusion protein with amino acids 5-304 of human PG (Cordingley, 1997). This antibody is highly specific for PG and does not cross react with β-catenin at appropriate dilutions (H. Cordingley and A. I. Magee unpublished). Membranes were washed four times (5 minutes each) with PBS containing 0.05% (v/v) Tween-20 and incubated with horseradish peroxidase-conjugated anti-rabbit or - mouse IgG antibody (Sigma) for 2 hours at room temperature. Filters were developed using the ECL system (Amersham).ImmunoprecipitationCells grown in 9 cm tissue culture dishes to about 80% confluence were washed in cold PBS and extracted on ice for 10 minutes with 300 μl of OG buffer (30 mM n-octyl-β-D-glucopyranoside (OG; Sigma) in 25 mM Tris-HCl, pH 7.5, with 1 mM CaCl2). The lysate was spun at 14,000 rpm at 4°C and the pellet was kept as the OG-insoluble fraction. Aliquots of the supernatant (OG-soluble fraction) were used to perform immunoprecipitation with rabbit antibodies against Dsg1 (Wheeler et al., 1991b), Dsc2 or PG (10 μl) and Protein A-Sepharose (20 μl) for 2 hours at 4°C. Immune complexes were pelleted by centrifugation (6,500 rpm for 1-2 minutes) and washed three times in OG buffer followed by one wash in 50 mM Tris-HCl, pH 6.8. Immunoprecipitated protein was eluted with SDS sample buffer and resolved by SDS-PAGE. After electrotransfer to nitrocellulose the immunoprecipitates were analyzed by immunoblotting with different primary antibodies.Cell aggregation assaysCell layers were dissociated to single cells with trypsin in the presence of calcium (TC treatment) as described by Takeichi (1977). In brief, cells were incubated with 0.015% (w/v) trypsin in HCMF (Hepes-buffered Ca2+, Mg2+-free Hanks’ solution) supplemented with 2 mM CaCl2 (HMF) at 37°C for 30-40 minutes and washed twice in HMF at 4°C. Aggregation of the dissociated cells was carried out in a 50 mm gridded Petri dish (Costar). Approximately 5×105 cells suspended in 2 ml DH10 (1:1 mixture of Dulbecco’s modified Eagle’s medium and Ham’s F-12 buffered with 15 mM Hepes), were incubated in dishes (precoated with 1% (w/v) BSA at 37°C for ∼2 hours) with gentle rotatory shaking (approximately 80 rpm) at 37°C for 30 minutes to 1 hour, as described by Nose et al. (1988). After appropriate periods of incubation, cells were fixed by the addition of glutaraldehyde to 2.5% (w/v) and observed on a Nikon Diaphot inverted microscope. L1-1 cells (Ozawa et al., 1990) expressing mouse E-cadherin, a kind gift of Dr Rolf Kemler, were used as positive controls. For quantitation, photographs were taken on 35 mm film (Ilford HP5) and enlarged prints prepared. Aggregates were treated as two-dimensional projections from which their average area was estimated by point counting. Each photograph was covered with a transparent overlay 13 cm × 9 cm in size consisting of rows and columns of points 5 mm apart. The area occupied by individual aggregates was measured by recording the number of intersections (p) made by the points with the groups of cells relative to the total number of points (P) within a known area. The fraction (p/P) yielded an estimate of the area of individual aggregates from which the mean area was obtained by pooling the measurements.To assay for co-aggregation, each cell population was labelled overnight with a distinct fluorescent dye, diI (3 μg/ml) or diO (15 μg/ml) (both from Molecular Probes), and was trypsinised using the same conditions as for the aggregation assay. Cells were then coincubated at a 1:1 ratio and allowed to form aggregates which were analysed using a Nikon Diaphot fluorescence microscope and results were recorded as pairs of colour pictures obtained with filters appropriate for rhodamine (for diI) and fluorescein (for diO).Fluorescence activated cell sorting (FACS) analysisSingle cell suspensions were prepared using the same conditions as for the aggregation assay. Cells were then washed twice and resuspended in PBS containing 0.5% (w/v) BSA and 0.05% (w/v) sodium azide (PBA). All subsequent washes and antibody incubations were performed at 4°C. Cells were incubated for 45 minutes in 100 μl of a 1:25 dilution (in PBA) of anti-Dsc2 polyclonal serum (King et al., 1993), washed three times and incubated for at least 30 minutes with 100 μl of a 1:50 dilution of FITC-conjugated goat anti-rabbit IgG (Sigma). Cells were then washed three times, resuspended in 0.3 to 0.5 ml of ice-cold filtered PBA and analyzed on a FACScan flow cytometer (Becton Dickinson) by Chris Atkins of the Immunology Division at NIMR.Immunoelectron microscopy and stereologyCells were grown on 35 mm diameter plastic dishes (Nunc, Denmark) and incubated at 4°C with a mixture of rabbit antisera against the extracellular domain of Dsc2 (King et al., 1993) and a synthetic peptide corresponding to residues 538-554 of mature human Dsc2 (King et al., 1995) at a diluton of 1:10 each in growth medium containing 0.1% Na azide for 1 hour. Cells were then washed on ice with four changes of PBS over a 15 minute period. Following 30 minutes fixation with 2% paraformaldehyde in PBS at room temperature (RT), samples were washed in 0.1 M NH4Cl in PBS (two changes, 10 minutes each) before incubation for 4-5 hours at RT, with occasional rocking, in goat anti-rabbit-10 nm gold conjugate (British Biocell International, Cardiff, UK), diluted 1:10 in 0.1 M Tris-HCl, pH 7.3, containing 0.5% fish skin gelatin (Sigma). Samples were washed with PBS (six changes over 30 minutes) before fixation in 2% paraformaldehyde-2% glutaraldehyde buffered with 0.1 M sodium cacodylate, pH 7.3, at 4°C overnight followed by postfixation with OsO4-uranyl acetate. During dehydration in ethanol, the cell layer on the surface of each dish was scored with a scalpel into rectangles with sides of 5-10 mm. The dish was dissolved with 1,2-epoxy-propane, freeing the individual rectangles as intact sheets of cells attached to their extracellular matrix, which were then transferred via a wide-bore pipette to polypropylene tubes, washed with several changes of 1,2-epoxy-propane over 1 hour and embedded in Araldite. About 10-15 sheets were obtained from each dish and orientated by low speed centrifugation at 3,000 rpm in a swing-out rotor of a Centra-3C centrifuge (IEC, Dunstable, Beds, UK) (see Griffiths et al., 1984; Burdett, 1993). Sections were stained with uranyl acetate and lead citrate and examined at 80 kV in a JEOL 1200EX electron microscope. This preserved in situ relationships between cells and enabled sampling of material from the entire dish surface to examine the distribution of immunogold label. Centrifugation of cell sheets ensured that 6-12 individual strips could be visualised in a single vertical section. In this way, the location of gold particles from a representative sample could be counted on apical and basal surfaces as well as along the lateral borders of neighbouring cells. For sampling purposes, vertical sections from each of two blocks per sample were picked up onto 100 mesh hexagonal grids bearing a pyroxylin-carbon film. Each strip of cells within a section was sampled in a systematic random manner (Weibel, 1979) to ensure that unlabelled and labelled cell profiles were detected with equal probability. Micrographs were taken along each strip of cells at regular intervals of 16 μm, using the stage controls to move sections by increments determined from the microscope’s x,y coordinate system. Sections were examined and photographed at a nominal magnification of ×6,000; the actual magnification was calibrated with a replica of a diffraction grating (2,160 lines/mm; E. F. Fullam Inc., Graticules Ltd, Tonbridge, Kent, UK). Counts of gold particles per unit length or area were performed on enlarged negatives, using a transparent square lattice overlay with a side (d) equal to 0.92 μm or 1.8 μm to count the intersections with profiles of the plasma membrane. The number of gold particles (N)/μm were then calculated from: N = ΣGi/(π/4 ·d·ΣIi) where ΣGi is the summation of the number of gold particles, ΣIi is that of intersection counts and π/4 is a correction factor for section thickness (see Weibel, 1979; Griffiths, 1993). For counts/μm2 the section thickness was determined by the fold procedure (Small, 1968). Ratio statistics were calculated as described by Cochran (1977) and levels of significance between mean values assessed by Student’s t-test from standard tables.Immunofluorescence microscopyAll steps were performed on ice. Cells on coverslips were extracted with OG buffer for 10 minutes, washed gently once with PBS and fixed for 30 minutes with 3% paraformaldehyde in PBS. Coverslips were washed gently twice with PBS and blocked with 3% BSA/1% glycine in PBS for at least two hours. Cells were incubated with rabbit anti-Dsc2 (1:25) or rabbit anti-Dsg (1:100) for 1 hour, washed gently three times with PBS, then stained with FITC-conjugated anti-rabbit antibodies for 1 hour followed by washing and mounting in Citifluor (Agar Scientific, UK). Cells were visualised on a Zeiss Axiomat microscope and photographed on Ilford HP5 film.RESULTSExpression and characterization of human desmocollin Dsc2a and human desmoglein Dsg1 in L cellsTo examine the function of the desmosomal cadherins in cell adhesion, L cells were transfected using two different mammalian expression vectors: pMSGgpt carrying the cDNA for human desmocollin Dsc2a, or pcDNAIneo carrying the cDNA for human desmoglein Dsg1. Transfected cells were grown in selective medium and resistant colonies were isolated and screened by PCR analysis using different sets of specific primers to confirm the presence of the appropriate cDNA inserts (data not shown). More than half of the DSC2a-transfected clones contained insert. PCR analysis of one of the DSG1-transfected clones which expressed Dsg1 protein showed the expected product band. Subsequent experiments were carried out using several independent clones for Dsc2a and the clone found to express Dsg1 at a detectable level.PCR-positive clones stably transfected with DSC2a cDNA were treated for 48 hours with dexamethasone (2 μM) to induce expression of the protein (∼120 kDa) which was detected by immunoblotting using a rabbit antiserum in all the clones while untreated clones and untransfected L cells showed little or no detectable expression of the protein (Fig. 1a). A non-specific band detected by this antibody migrated in the position of Dsc2b but was present in untransfected cells and unaffected by dexamethasone induction. This does not appear to be Dsc2b since other Dsc antibodies do not recognise it and there is no reason to expect Dsc to be expressed in these cells. A mouse monoclonal antibody against human Dsg1 stained a band of the predicted size (∼150 kDa) in only one of the DSG1 cDNA transfectants on immunoblot analysis (Fig. 1b). Different DSC2a transfectants had similar expression levels of Dsc2a, but the levels of expression of Dsc2a in these and of Dsg1 in the DSG1 transfectant were severalfold lower than the expression of the same molecules in bona fide epithelial cell lines used routinely as positive controls (TR 131, MDCK, A431; Fig. 1 lanes T and data not shown). This may account for the low signal-to-noise ratio seen in immunoblots. Transfectants expressing either construct showed fibroblastic morphology similar to parental L cells, although they tended to show a flattened shape compared with untransfected L cells, particularly when treated with dexamethasone. Bar, 400 μm.Dsc2a- and Dsg1-expressing cells co-aggregateSince desmosomal proteins normally function in a multi-molecular assembly containing roughly equal amounts of desmocollins and desmogleins, the proteins expressed individually might be less functional, which could explain the weak aggregation activity observed using singly transfected clones. To test this, and whether heterophilic binding between Dsc2a and Dsg1 could be detected, co-aggregation experiments were performed. Dexamethasone-induced Dsc2a-expressing single clones and Dsg1-expressing cells were labelled separately with the fluorescent dyes diI or diO, trypsinized in the presence of Ca2+, mixed and allowed to aggregate under the same conditions used for the previous aggregation assays, followed by observation under a fluorescence microscope using filters appropriate for the two marker dyes. The two types of cell clearly co-aggregated as evidenced by the presence of cells labelled with both dyes in the same aggregates (Fig. 4). These data demonstrate heterophilic adhesion between Dsc2a- and Dsg1-expressing cells. To test whether PG expression could enhance the cell-cell adhesion activity of desmosomal cadherins, a clone of Dsg1/Dsc2a-expressing L cells was further co-transfected with PG cDNA in the pcDNAIneo vector with pHygr as a co-selectable marker, followed by selection in hygromycin and cloning. (1994). No effect of PG expression on the level of Dsg1 was observed.When triply transfected DSG1/DSC2a/PG cells were tested after dexamethasone induction in the standard cell-cell aggregation assay, a dramatic aggregation was observed which resulted in rapid formation of very large aggregates involving a high proportion of cells in the assay (Fig. 6). Aggregates were larger and more extensive even than those produced by positive control E-cadherin-expressing L1-1 cells, although the latter cells had not been regularly selected for maximal expression of E-cadherin and therefore aggregated to a lesser extent than previously reported (Ozawa et al., 1990). The size of aggregates was quite variable, as reflected in the error bars, but average values for the projected area were 9- to 14-fold greater than those of single or double transfectants (Fig. 6c). Uninduced cells aggregated to a much lower extent comparable with single transfectants (not shown). As a measure of the efficiency of aggregation of the three cell types the ratio of the projected area of aggregates, as shown in Fig. 6c, to the percentage of cells involved in aggregates (calculated as the number of aggregates per microscope field divided by the number of single cells) was calculated. At t=30 minutes the figures for single, double and triple transfectants were 0.11, 0.21 and 2.49 and at t=60 minutes they were 0.08, 0.36 and 5.21, respectively. Thus double transfectants aggregated only 1.9-4.5 times better than singly transfected cells, whereas triple transfectants aggregated 22-65 and 12-14 times better than single and double transfectants, respectively.Immunoelectron microscopic localisation of Dsc2a on surfaces of transfected cellsThe dramatic cell-cell aggregation activity of triply transfected cells could be due to PG co-expression causing a quantitative increase in the amount of desmosomal cadherins on the cell surface. This was tested for Dsc2a, for which antibodies to the extracellular domain are available, using an immunogold procedure that allowed both quantitation of cell surface antigen and observation of the spatial distribution of the label. Live cells were incubated with a mixture of rabbit antisera against the extracellular domain of Dsc2 and against a synthetic peptide corresponding to residues 538-554 of mature human Dsc2 for maximum sensitivity. After binding of antibodies to the cell surface, cells were washed, fixed and bound antibodies detected with gold-conjugated secondary antibody. Gold particles could be clearly seen on the surface of transfected cells after dexamethasone induction (Fig. 7). Particles were found both individually and clustered in small groups, but there was no apparent difference in degree of clustering between singly- or multiply transfected cells. Quantitative analysis of the data (Table 1) revealed a signal above background of 0.28-0.5 gold particles/μm2 of surface area for uninduced cells. This increased to 2.29-3.94 gold particles/μm2 in induced cells, an increase of 5.3- to 12-fold. Comparison of singly- and doubly transfected cells in the same experiment did not reveal a significant difference (10.3-fold versus 12.3-fold above uninduced cells, respectively). Triply transfected cells also showed similar levels of cell surface Dsc2a. Multiple independent clones, referred to as Zeo clones, were isolated which were shown to express Dsc2a to very similar levels after dexamethasone induction and also to express similar amounts of PG (data not shown). Dsg1 expression levels, however, varied over approximately a 100-fold range, the highest expressers approaching levels found in positive control TR 131 squamous cell carcinoma cells (data not shown). Clones with similar Dsg1 expression levels to the earlier triple transfectants were chosen for subsequent studies; these also demonstrated comparable adhesive properties i.e. extensive and rapid aggregation (data not shown).To examine interactions between PG and desmosomal cadherins, immunoprecipitation experiments were performed on Zeo clones using OG lysates (Fig. 8). In DSC2a/DSG1/PG cells, immunoprecipitation of either Dsg1 or Dsc2a from the OG-soluble fraction resulted in co-precipitation of PG but not the other cadherin. When PG antibody was used in immunoprecipitation both desmosomal cadherins were co-precipitated. These results indicated that PG can form OG-soluble binary complexes with either Dsc2a or Dsg1, but ternary complexes are not detected. Similarly, these data do not provide any evidence for Dsg1-Dsc2a complexes in the OG-soluble fraction. However, most of the three proteins were still present in the OG-insoluble fraction (Fig. 8) suggesting that there might be an interaction with the cytoskeleton. Localisation of the OG-insoluble desmosomal cadherins by immunofluorescence microscopy (Fig. 9) showed punctate concentrations at cell borders, often at sites of contact.
